title: Thorax: Surface Anatomy, Pleura and Mediastinum
introduction: The thorax is the region between the neck and the abdomen enclosing an irregularly shaped cylindrical cavity bounded by musculoskeletal walls and the diaphragm[cite: 61]. Internally, the central mediastinum separates two lateral pulmonary cavities, housing the heart, great vessels, lungs, esophagus, and major lymphatic trunks[cite: 61].
learningOutcomes: 7.1 Describe the musculoskeletal boundaries of the thoracic wall and the asymmetrical dome levels of the diaphragm[cite: 61].
7.2 Explain the pleural membranes, pleural sleeve, pulmonary ligament, and clinical pleural cavity disorders[cite: 61].
7.3 Outline the subdivisions, boundaries, contents, and fascial spaces of the mediastinum[cite: 61].
7.4 Identify the anterior, posterior, left, and right anatomical relations of the thoracic esophagus[cite: 61].
7.5 Trace the course, relations, and branches of the thoracic aorta alongside the drainage territories of the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct[cite: 61].

content.heading: Thoracic Wall and the Diaphragm
content.body: The thoracic wall consists anteriorly of the sternum (manubrium, body, and xiphoid process), posteriorly of the 12 thoracic vertebrae and their intervertebral discs, laterally of the ribs, costal cartilages, and muscles spanning adjacent intercostal spaces, and inferiorly of the diaphragm[cite: 61]. Key surface reference lines include the anterior median (midsternal) line, midclavicular lines, and anterior, mid-, and posterior axillary lines, alongside bony landmarks such as the jugular (suprasternal) notch, sternal angle (Angle of Louis at the 2nd costal cartilage and T4 level), C7 spinous process (vertebra prominens), and the superior angle of the scapula at T2[cite: 61]. The diaphragm is a double-domed musculotendinous partition at the inferior thoracic aperture separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities into right and left hemidiaphragms[cite: 61]. Because the large right lobe of the liver pushes it superiorly, the right hemidiaphragm dome projects slightly higher than the left, lying approximately at the 5th rib anteriorly during complete normal expiration while standing[cite: 61]. The left hemidiaphragm dome sits at the inferior border of the 5th rib at the midclavicular line, which corresponds to the T8 vertebral level[cite: 61].

content.heading: Pulmonary Cavities, Pleura, and Clinical Anatomy
content.body: The thoracic cavity contains three subdivisions: the central mediastinum and two lateral pulmonary cavities[cite: 61]. Each pulmonary cavity is lined by parietal pleura and encloses a lung, its visceral pleura, and the intervening pleural cavity[cite: 61]. Mediastinal parietal pleura continues laterally over the root of the lung as the pleural sleeve and projects inferiorly as a double-layered fold called the pulmonary ligament (inferior pulmonary ligament), which connects the mediastinum (anterior to the esophagus), lung root, and lower lung to anchor the lung base and allow pulmonary vein expansion[cite: 61]. Serous fluid inside the pleural cavity generates surface tension and cohesion that keeps the lung against the thoracic wall during breathing; disruption of this cohesion causes elastic lung collapse (atelectasis)[cite: 61]. Clinical disorders include pneumothorax (air in the pleural cavity from spontaneous rupture, lung disease, trauma, or chest tube procedures—appearing black on chest X-ray), pleural effusion (excess fluid preventing lung expansion—appearing white/gray on chest X-ray), and hemothorax (blood in the pleural cavity from trauma, ruptured vessels, malignancy, or anticoagulation for pulmonary embolism—also appearing white/gray on chest X-ray)[cite: 61].

content.heading: Subdivisions of the Mediastinum and Mediastinal Spaces
content.body: The mediastinum extends from the sternum anteriorly to the vertebral column posteriorly, and from the thoracic inlet above to the diaphragm below, dividing into the superior mediastinum and the inferior mediastinum (anterior, middle, and posterior)[cite: 61]. The superior mediastinum extends from the thoracic inlet to a plane passing from the sternal angle anteriorly to the lower border of T4 posteriorly; its superficial layer contains the thymus, left and right brachiocephalic veins, and superior vena cava, while its middle layer contains the aortic arch with its three branches, phrenic nerves, and vagus nerves[cite: 61]. Within the inferior mediastinum, the anterior mediastinum lies behind the sternal body and costal cartilages and anterior to the pericardium, containing fat, thymus remnants, and anterior mediastinal lymph nodes[cite: 61]. The middle mediastinum lies between the anterior and posterior subdivisions and contains the heart and pericardium, the roots/terminations of the great vessels, phrenic nerves, pericardiacophrenic vessels, and lymph nodes[cite: 61]. The posterior mediastinum lies behind the heart and pericardium and anterior to vertebrae T5 to T12, housing the esophagus, vagus nerves, thoracic aorta, azygos venous system, thoracic duct, thoracic sympathetic trunk, and posterior mediastinal lymph nodes[cite: 61]. Three key mediastinal spaces are described: the retrosternal space (between the sternum and endothoracic fascia), the pretracheal space (within the superior mediastinum between the trachea, tracheal bifurcation, and aortic arch), and the retroesophageal space (within the superior mediastinum between the esophagus and endothoracic fascia)[cite: 61].

content.heading: Anatomical Relations of the Thoracic Esophagus
content.body: As the esophagus descends through the mediastinum, it maintains close relations on all four sides[cite: 61]. Anteriorly, it is related to the trachea, tracheal bifurcation, left principal bronchus, left recurrent laryngeal nerve, right pulmonary artery, anterior esophageal plexus, pericardium, left atrium, and diaphragm[cite: 61]. Posteriorly, it lies anterior to the posterior esophageal plexus, thoracic aorta, thoracic duct, azygos vein, hemiazygos vein, accessory hemiazygos vein, and right posterior intercostal veins[cite: 61]. On its left lie the left common carotid artery, left subclavian artery, aortic arch, thoracic aorta, and the superior part of the thoracic duct[cite: 61]. On its right, it is directly related to the arch of the azygos vein[cite: 61].

content.heading: The Thoracic Aorta
content.body: The thoracic aorta continues from the aortic arch at the lower border of T4, descends on the left side of and then anterior to the vertebral column, and passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at the T12 vertebral level to enter the abdomen[cite: 61]. Its relations include the left lung root, pericardium, and esophagus anteriorly; the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins posteriorly; the azygos vein and thoracic duct to the right; and the mediastinal pleura to the left[cite: 61]. Its parietal branches comprise nine pairs of posterior intercostal arteries, one pair of subcostal arteries (supplying the lower nine intercostal spaces and upper abdominal wall), and superior phrenic arteries (supplying the superior surface of the diaphragm)[cite: 61]. Its visceral branches comprise one or two bronchial branches for each lung, esophageal branches, and pericardial branches[cite: 61].

content.heading: Thoracic Duct and Right Lymphatic Duct
content.body: The thoracic duct begins anterior to L1 as a dilated sac called the cisterna chyli, formed by the union of the left and right lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk[cite: 61]. It enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm, ascends anterior to the vertebral column between the thoracic aorta and azygos vein, veers to the left at T5, and arches forward at the root of the neck to empty into the left venous angle[cite: 61]. Just before terminating, it receives the left jugular, left subclavian, and left bronchomediastinal trunks, draining lymph from the lower limbs, pelvic cavity, abdominal cavity, left side of the thorax, left head and neck, and left upper limb[cite: 61]. The right lymphatic duct is formed by the union of the right jugular, right subclavian, and right bronchomediastinal trunks, enters the right venous angle, and drains lymph from the right half of the head, neck, thorax, and right upper limb[cite: 61].

inTextQuestions.question: Why does the dome of the right hemidiaphragm sit slightly higher than the left hemidiaphragm?
inTextQuestions.answer: Because the large right lobe of the liver pushes the right hemidiaphragm superiorly[cite: 61].

inTextQuestions.question: How do air (pneumothorax) and fluid (hemothorax or pleural effusion) differ in appearance on a chest X-ray?
inTextQuestions.answer: Air in a pneumothorax appears black on a chest X-ray, whereas fluid in a hemothorax or pleural effusion appears white or gray[cite: 61].

inTextQuestions.question: At which vertebral levels does the thoracic aorta begin and pass through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm?
inTextQuestions.answer: It begins as a continuation of the aortic arch at the lower border of T4 and passes through the aortic hiatus at the level of the T12 vertebra[cite: 61].

inTextQuestions.question: At which vertebral level does the thoracic duct veer to the left, and where does it terminate?
inTextQuestions.answer: It veers to the left at the level of T5 and terminates by entering the left venous angle[cite: 61].

saqs.question: State the boundaries of the thoracic wall and specify the vertebral level corresponding to the 5th rib at the midclavicular line.
saqs.answer: The thoracic wall is bounded anteriorly by the sternum, posteriorly by the 12 thoracic vertebrae and intervertebral discs, laterally by the ribs, costal cartilages, and intercostal muscles, and inferiorly by the diaphragm[cite: 61]. The level of the 5th rib at the midclavicular line corresponds to the T8 vertebral level[cite: 61].

saqs.question: Define the pleural sleeve and pulmonary ligament, and state the two main functions of the pulmonary ligament.
saqs.answer: The pleural sleeve is the mediastinal parietal pleura continuing laterally to surround the root of the lung, and the pulmonary ligament is the double-layer of pleura projecting inferiorly from the pleural sleeve[cite: 61]. It anchors the lower region of each lung and allows for vascular expansion of the pulmonary veins[cite: 61].

saqs.question: Differentiate between pneumothorax, pleural effusion, and hemothorax, and explain why breaking pleural cohesion causes atelectasis.
saqs.answer: Pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity, pleural effusion is excessive fluid in the pleural cavity, and hemothorax is blood in the pleural cavity[cite: 61]. Serous fluid normally creates surface tension that holds the visceral and parietal pleura together; when air, fluid, or blood breaks that cohesion, the lung collapses (atelectasis) due to its natural elastic properties[cite: 61].

saqs.question: List the contents of the middle mediastinum and the posterior mediastinum.
saqs.answer: Middle mediastinum: heart and pericardium, beginning or termination of the great vessels, phrenic nerves, pericardiacophrenic vessels, and lymph nodes[cite: 61]. Posterior mediastinum: esophagus, vagus nerves, thoracic aorta, azygos system of veins, thoracic duct, thoracic sympathetic trunk, and posterior mediastinal lymph nodes[cite: 61].

saqs.question: Compare the origin, termination, and drainage territories of the thoracic duct and the right lymphatic duct.
saqs.answer: The thoracic duct begins anterior to L1 at the cisterna chyli, empties into the left venous angle, and drains the lower limbs, pelvis, abdomen, left thorax, left head and neck, and left upper limb[cite: 61]. The right lymphatic duct forms from the union of the right jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks, empties into the right venous angle, and drains the right half of the head, neck, thorax, and right upper limb[cite: 61].
